title: To whom shall we go? (John 6:52–71)
hookLine: many leave; Peter says: you have the words of eternal life

cards: There's a moment in a lot of friendships, and a lot of faiths, when the thing gets hard. Something is said that you can't quite follow, or can't quite accept. You look around, and other people are quietly leaving.
This is that moment in John's Gospel.
In the synagogue at Capernaum, Jesus's teaching about bread from heaven gets stranger and stronger, and even his own followers mutter among themselves: "This is an hard saying; who can hear it?"

teach.h: EAT MY FLESH, DRINK MY BLOOD.
teach.b: What was so hard? Jesus had said that unless they eat his flesh and drink his blood, they have no life in them. His hearers take it as literally as anyone would, and they recoil.

teach.h: CHURCHES HEAR IT IN DIFFERENT WAYS.
teach.b: Christians have understood these words in different ways ever since. Catholic and Orthodox Christians hear in them the Eucharist, the bread and wine that become, in their teaching, the body and blood of Christ.
Lutherans speak of Christ truly present in the bread and wine. Other Protestant churches read the words as a picture of faith: taking Christ in, the way bread is taken into the body.

teach.h: MANY WALKED NO MORE WITH HIM.
teach.b: In the story, the result is the same: "From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him." Not enemies. Disciples.
So Jesus turns to the twelve: "Will ye also go away?" He doesn't beg them to stay. He doesn't soften what he said.

teach.h: LORD, TO WHOM SHALL WE GO?
teach.b: And Peter answers for them: "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life." Listen to how honest that is. Peter doesn't say I understand everything, or it was easy to hear.
He says, where else would we go? It isn't certainty. It's a choice about where life is, made on a day he doesn't understand everything.
And John adds a sad note: Jesus already knows one of the twelve will betray him.

how: Some Christians turn to Peter's words in seasons of doubt, and in some liturgies his line is sung as a verse before the Gospel is read.

games.q: many followers have just walked away, and Jesus turns to you: will you also go away? what do you say?
o: "we'll stay if you explain it better."
games.why: Peter: "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life." not certainty, but knowing where life is.

practice: Think of something that gives you life but has gotten hard lately: a friendship, a marriage, a practice like this one, a faith if you have one.
Notice whether part of you wants to walk away quietly, and without scolding it, ask Peter's question: if I leave, where would I go?
If you pray, tell God plainly what's hard; if you don't, hold the thing that gives you life, and choose it for today.
